verdicts.critic:
Steelman review of "Vaccine Mandates & Public Health Authority" — six camps, each read against the test "would a real proponent sign this as their strongest case?"

Five of six pass that test comfortably. The banner lines are all in-voice and quotable, the Guardian, Conscience Broadener, Confidence Builder, Medical Freedom and Institutional Risk Owner sections each carry their own evidence, name real proponents, and close on their own terms after answering the obvious objection. No house verdict, no forced 50/50: asymmetry is carried by prevalence weights and the Crux rather than by an editorial thumb. No major camp is missing — school-entry hardliners, religious-exemption litigators, vaccine-by-vaccine minimalists, persuasion-first public health, absolutist consent, and institutional risk-owners cover the live US field, and the fragmenting-authority question is carried in Basics and the questions rather than needing a seventh camp.

The Schedule Minimalist is the one softened side. It is the only camp whose section hands the last word to an opponent: the Hib/pneumococcal "proves too much" rebuttal stands unanswered, its flagship source (Opel/Diekema/Marcuse 2008) is disclaimed mid-paragraph as not actually supporting the camp's policy, and its third paragraph closes on a coalition embarrassment. Net effect for a reader: nobody credible holds this view. That is a structural defect, not a phrasing quibble, and it is compounded because part of the disclaimer overstates what those authors wrote.

On sourcing, most of the load-bearing in-position material checks out against primary sources: SB277's 2.37%→0.56% personal-belief drop (Delamater, Pediatrics 2019), the AAP's August 2025 policy statement and its "creates unnecessary risk to both individuals and communities" language, the Marine Corps 0.52% and Navy 1.02% approval rates, the 2024 Navy settlement's $1,500,000 attorney-fee term and FY2025-27 promotion-board bar, Miller v. McDonald decided against the Amish families June 30, 2026 on remand, the 198 denied St. Louis religious requests and Becket's Eighth Circuit amicus, PromoVac's 75.9% vs 68.6% at seven months and the separately published 40% hesitancy reduction, the +5-point announcement-training HPV gain, Opel 2008's tenth criterion verbatim, AAPS's July 8 1999 "not spread by casual contact" release naming Ohio's law, the IDSA/SHEA/PIDS December 2013 joint statement including the 90% threshold and "condition of employment, unpaid service, or receipt of professional privileges," the AHA's July 21 2021 statement verbatim, VICP totals, the ~1,780 NYC terminations, Florida's August 2026 proposed rule, HHS OCR's September 4 2025 VFC letter, WV SB 26 and SB 237, and Arizona HCR 2056's special-health-care-district carve-out (House third reading 3/2/2026).

notes: Label/value scope mismatch, non-blocking: "Coverage change after ending non-medical exemptions · California" carries value 95.1%, which is the after-level, not the change (+2.3 pp). A scanner reading the big number against the word "change" can misparse it. The note ("rose from 92.8 percent to 95.1 percent") and the before/after series bars are both in the compact layer, so the reader is corrected in the same glance — hence not blocking. If touched: "Coverage after ending non-medical exemptions · California, 2017-18".

"US measles cases in 2025 · worst year in three decades" is internally undercut by its own compact note, "2026 has already run higher than 2025" — if 2026 is higher, 2025 is not the worst year. Separately, the fact that makes 2,288 matter (the US is highly likely to lose measles elimination status when it is reassessed in November 2026) lives only in the detail; it is even the source's own headline. One reword fixes both, e.g. note: "Cases cluster in unvaccinated communities rather than spreading evenly; 2026 is running higher still, and the US is on track to lose its measles-elimination status this fall."

Exemption-design structure sits entirely below the fold: "States allowing a religious or philosophical exemption · out of 50" (T2) carries that all 50 states require core vaccines, that all 50 + DC allow a medical exemption, and that 45 + DC add a non-medical one. Above the fold the reader infers state variation only indirectly, from the California stat and the coverage range (Idaho 75.2% / West Virginia 98.9%). The ▲ six are each strong enough that no swap is obviously right, and Basics is a 3-col grid (a seventh breaks the row), so this stays a note — but if a slot ever opens, this is the strongest promotion candidate in the section.

"Kindergartners exempted from a vaccine · national rate" (4.2%) never says in the compact layer that roughly 4.0 of those 4.2 points are non-medical; that split is in the detail. A reader could assume medical exemptions drive the rise. Partially rescued above the fold by the California stat, whose note names "religious and personal-belief exemptions" as the thing eliminated, so non-blocking.

The crux subtitle enumerates six accounts of what a mandate must answer to, for seven camps; the missing one is Hassle Factor Architect's (make the exemption cost effort). It reads fine as prose rather than as a claim of completeness, but worth re-reading after the positions reorder above — with Medical Freedom Campaigner promoted, the one bar the subtitle names without a visible card becomes visible, and the only unlisted account is the one that drops below.

Questions fold is well-placed: the four ▲ questions cover does-it-work, the autonomy clash, which-diseases-qualify, and who-decides — the four axes the position set actually splits on. prevalence_basis.name: Herd Immunity Guardian
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: Every state has school-entry requirements and the major pediatric and infectious-disease societies back them; 29 states plus DC rejected the loosened 2026 federal schedule, though only about six states permit medical exemptions alone.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Measles needs roughly 95% coverage to stop, and school-entry rules with medical exemptions only are the one tool proven to hold that line.

prevalence_basis.name: Conscience Exemption Broadener
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: Religious exemptions are law in about 44 states and DC and philosophical ones in roughly 15; a 2025 KFF/Washington Post parent survey found 44% calling vaccination a parent’s personal choice, and religious-exemption suits are live at state supreme court level.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Keep the requirements, but a state that overrides sincere religious or parental conviction has crossed a line no health benefit buys back.

prevalence_basis.name: Schedule Minimalist
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: Holds the federal advisory machinery since the 2025 reconstitution of ACIP and drives state health-department rulemaking to trim required vaccines, though a federal court stayed the reduced 2026 schedule in March.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Compel only where the disease is severe and spreads in classrooms; hepatitis B at birth and chickenpox never belonged on a school-entry list.

prevalence_basis.name: Vaccine Confidence Builder
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: Dominant in vaccine-hesitancy scholarship and international health-agency behavioral guidance, with almost no legislative footprint of its own; cited by mandate supporters and opponents alike.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Coercion buys short-run compliance and long-run distrust; access, outreach, and trusted clinicians raise uptake without the backlash.

prevalence_basis.name: Medical Freedom Campaigner
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: Roughly 15 states bar vaccine mandates for state employees, Idaho enacted a broad medical-freedom act in 2025, and about 30% of parents in a 2025 KFF/Washington Post survey favored removing school requirements entirely.
prevalence_basis.sketch: No procedure carrying any risk should be the price of a classroom seat or a paycheck; consent is meaningless without the right to refuse.

prevalence_basis.name: Hassle Factor Architect
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: Already the operating design in Michigan, Washington, Oregon, and Vermont, and argued directly against the AAP’s elimination call by two pediatric bioethicists in JAMA Pediatrics.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Keep nonmedical exemptions but price them in effort — counseling visits and education modules recover most of the coverage elimination would buy, without the political risk.
